newsitem.title: USA: Skepticism over US budget balance pervades Wall St.
newsitem.headline: Skepticism over US budget balance pervades Wall St.

text.p: Despite a post-election burst of optimism, Wall Street remains dubious over prospects for further cuts in the federal budget from the Democratic White House and the Republican-led Congress.

"Despite the election-year rhetoric we heard, I don't think there are going to be proposals to start moving towards a balanced budget," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
Attempts to cut spending must include drastic reforms in entitlements such as Medicare and Medicaid, analysts said.
However, the future envisioned for those programs by Republicans is virtually the opposite of the Democratic strategy. And that gap is not expected to be closed soon.

"You're not going to see anything happen quickly ... I expect it's really not going to be until the latter half of 1997 at the earliest before they even begin discussing moving toward a balanced budget," Moran said.
The future of Medicare was one of the main divergencies between the platforms of President Clinton and Republican contender Bob Dole during the presidential run.

"The fact the President beat up the Republicans so much on the issue of entitlements ... is going to make it very difficult for any sort of reasonable compromise in slowing the rate of growth in Medicare spending going forward," said David Hensley, economist at Salomon Brothers Inc.
But not all the market's hopes have been dashed.
Analysts pointed to recent speeches touting "cooperation and responsibility" from Democrats and Republicans alike.
The two sides, they said, seem to have learned the lesson that pure confrontation and radical opinions one way or the other will not cut it with American voters.
President Clinton spent the first two years of his administration trying to implement a Democratic, more left-wing political agenda and mostly failed.
Republicans seized control of Congress in 1994, but failed to enact the most conservative parts of their "Contract with America" such as slower growth in Medicare spending.
After two government shutdowns during last year's budget crisis, Clinton and the Republicans agreed to disagree.
Current pledges of cooperation are "sort of typical post-election hangover, and it might not last for too long," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.

"But certainly the momentum is there ... I think that if Clinton wants to solve these problems he's got an opportunity. But the trick is they have to start working on this before the animosity returns ... and it inevitably will," Low added.
Analysts said a strong economy gives Clinton and Congress a window to cut the deficit, even if growth slows a bit in 1997.
But Salomon Brother's Hensley warned "If the economy decelerates you're going to see at least somewhat slower revenue growth and possibly a deterioration of the spending side."
This, he said, "would make it more difficult to keep the momentum behind closing the (budget) gap."
Analysts said the fact that Clinton is now a second-term president may also be a positive in the budget process.

"Second-term presidents are not thinking about re-election anymore, they're thinking about history books," Low said. "If Clinton could fix the entitlement situation that, would be a tremendous achievement."
